title: Need for evaluation methods for likelihood-free generative models
description: Generative models that can sample but cannot estimate likelihood directly motivate further research into how to evaluate such models.
canonical_description: evaluation methods needed for generative models that sample without likelihood estimation

evidence.anchor: further research into how to evaluate such models
evidence.quote:
Advances in generative models that can sample but not estimate likelihood directly motivate further research
into how to evaluate such models.

verdict.reasoning: The gap asks for evaluation methods for generative models that sample without likelihood estimation, and the subsequent literature supplies multiple direct solutions. PQMass provides a general, likelihood-free statistical framework that compares model and reference samples via Voronoi-region multinomial counts and Pearson chi-squared tests, requiring only distances, and is validated across images, tabular data, time series, and protein sequences with asymptotic consistency guarantees. The optimized Maximum Mean Discrepancy paper contributes a two-sample test with power-optimized kernels, permutation null estimation, and witness visualization, validated on a real likelihood-free GAN. The latent-density-score paper adds a per-sample quality signal for latent-based generators (VAE, GAN, latent diffusion) without any pretrained feature extractor. Together these establish concrete, empirically validated methods for exactly the setting in the gap. Remaining caveats — i.i.d. sample requirements, reliance on a meaningful distance/kernel, needing a reference dataset or an encodable latent space, and limited coverage of modalities like language or correlated samplers — are limitations of individual methods rather than an unaddressed core problem; the canonical need for likelihood-free evaluation is substantially met. Confidence is high but not maximal because no single method is universal and a few modality-specific settings remain thinner.

paper.title: PQMass: Probabilistic Assessment of the Quality of Generative Models using Probability Mass Estimation
paper.abstract: We propose a likelihood-free method for comparing two distributions given samples from each, with the goal of assessing the quality of generative models. The proposed approach, PQMass, provides a statistically rigorous method for assessing the performance of a single generative model or the comparison of multiple competing models. PQMass divides the sample space into non-overlapping regions and applies chi-squared tests to the number of data samples that fall within each region, giving a p-value that measures the probability that the bin counts derived from two sets of samples are drawn from the same multinomial distribution. PQMass does not depend on assumptions regarding the density of the true distribution, nor does it rely on training or fitting any auxiliary models. We evaluate PQMass on data of various modalities and dimensions, demonstrating its effectiveness in assessing the quality, novelty, and diversity of generated samples. We further show that PQMass scales well to moderately high-dimensional data and thus obviates the need for feature extraction in practical applications.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes PQMass, a likelihood-free statistical framework for evaluating generative models by comparing two sets of samples (model-generated vs. reference). It partitions the space into Voronoi regions, counts how many samples fall in each region (a multinomial summary), and uses Pearson chi-squared tests to obtain a p-value assessing whether the two sample sets come from the same distribution. The method requires only distances between points — no likelihood, no density assumptions, and no auxiliary model fitting — which is exactly the setting described by the gap (generative models that sample but cannot estimate likelihood). The paper validates it empirically across modalities (sampling benchmarks, MNIST/CIFAR/FFHQ/ImageNet images, astrophysics images, time series, tabular data, protein sequences) and gives consistency guarantees that the test distinguishes distinct distributions asymptotically.
assessments.what_remains_open: The specific problem — providing an evaluation method for likelihood-free generative models — is substantially solved by this single well-tested proposal. Still, the paper itself documents residual gaps in coverage: the formalism requires i.i.d. samples (so models producing correlated samples cannot be evaluated); results are too noisy when sample counts are limited; effectiveness depends on a meaningful distance metric (nontrivial for modalities such as natural language); and novelty/memorization is only measured indirectly (via a two-sided/overfit p-value and generalization gap) rather than as a direct scalar. These are limitations of one method rather than an unaddressed part of the core problem.

paper.title: Generative Models and Model Criticism via Optimized Maximum Mean Discrepancy
paper.abstract: We propose a method to optimize the representation and distinguishability of samples from two probability distributions, by maximizing the estimated power of a statistical test based on the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD). This optimized MMD is applied to the setting of unsupervised learning by generative adversarial networks (GAN), in which a model attempts to generate realistic samples, and a discriminator attempts to tell these apart from data samples. In this context, the MMD may be used in two roles: first, as a discriminator, either directly on the samples, or on features of the samples. Second, the MMD can be used to evaluate the performance of a generative model, by testing the model's samples against a reference data set. In the latter role, the optimized MMD is particularly helpful, as it gives an interpretable indication of how the model and data distributions differ, even in cases where individual model samples are not easily distinguished either by eye or by classifier.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper develops an evaluation method for likelihood-free generative models (specifically GANs that sample but cannot compute likelihoods): an optimized Maximum Mean Discrepancy two-sample test whose kernel/features are chosen by maximizing test power, together with efficient permutation null-distribution computation and witness-function visualization for model criticism. It demonstrates this evaluation approach on a real semi-supervised GAN trained on MNIST (discretized to {0,1}^{28x28}), showing it detects distributional discrepancies (e.g., overproduction of certain digit types and pixel-level artifacts) that human observers and the median-heuristic RBF MMD would miss, and also proposes MMD-based GAN training criteria.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper's solution is an evaluation methodology based on two-sample hypothesis testing of a trained model's samples against a reference data set. It does not address evaluation in settings where no reference data set or clean data/model distinction exists, nor does it provide a full comparative benchmark across many models or cover other evaluation facets (e.g., coverage/recall-style metrics, diversity-mode collapse quantification beyond what MMD captures, or evaluation without any available true samples). Within reference-data sample-based evaluation for likelihood-free generative models, the paper does substantially solve the stated problem and validates it empirically.
evidence_snippets: In light of these varied approaches to discriminator training, it is important to be able to evaluate quality of samples from a generator against reference data.
Second, the \acro{mmd} can be used to evaluate the performance of a generative model, by testing the model's samples against a reference data set.
As an example of a real-world two-sample testing problem, we will consider distinguishing the output of a generative model from the reference distribution it attempts to reproduce.

paper.title: Assessing Sample Quality via the Latent Space of Generative Models
paper.abstract: Advances in generative models increase the need for sample quality assessment. To do so, previous methods rely on a pre-trained feature extractor to embed the generated samples and real samples into a common space for comparison. However, different feature extractors might lead to inconsistent assessment outcomes. Moreover, these methods are not applicable for domains where a robust, universal feature extractor does not yet exist, such as medical images or 3D assets. In this paper, we propose to directly examine the latent space of the trained generative model to infer generated sample quality. This is feasible because the quality a generated sample directly relates to the amount of training data resembling it, and we can infer this information by examining the density of the latent space. Accordingly, we use a latent density score function to quantify sample quality. We show that the proposed score correlates highly with the sample quality for various generative models including VAEs, GANs and Latent Diffusion Models. Compared with previous quality assessment methods, our method has the following advantages: 1) pre-generation quality estimation with reduced computational cost, 2) generalizability to various domains and modalities, and 3) applicability to latent-based image editing and generation methods. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed methods can benefit downstream tasks such as few-shot image classification and latent face image editing. Code is available at https://github.com/cvlab-stonybrook/LS-sample-quality.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes an evaluation method for exactly the class of models in the gap: generative models (VAEs, GANs, Latent Diffusion Models, Stable Diffusion) that generate samples without providing likelihood estimates. Rather than requiring likelihood or a pretrained feature extractor, it scores each generated sample by the density of training-set latent codes around the sample's latent code in the generative model's own latent space ("latent density score"). The authors validate that this score correlates with per-sample visual quality, precision/recall, realism score, and truncation level, and show it generalizes to domains without universal feature extractors (medical/anime images, 3D shapes) and enables downstream tasks (few-shot classification, latent face editing). This directly provides an evaluation method for likelihood-free generative models.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper fills the gap for instance-wise/per-sample quality assessment of latent-based likelihood-free generators, but it does not cover all ways one might "evaluate" such models. It does not provide a model-wise, distribution-level comparison metric (e.g., a FID-like aggregate of the whole generative distribution versus the real distribution); its score is a per-sample ranking/quality signal. Moreover, the method requires access to a generative model with a well-defined latent space into which real training samples can be encoded (or otherwise mapped to latent codes) plus a set of training latent codes, so it is not applicable to samplers lacking an encodable/invertible latent space or where training latent codes are unavailable. The authors explicitly leave high-dimensional latent models (e.g., deep hierarchical VAEs) and video/temporal latent generative models to future work, noting latent dimension reduction "might be a potential solution." For the core stated problem—evaluating models that sample without likelihood—the paper offers a concrete, validated solution.
evidence_snippets: we propose to directly examine the latent space of the trained generative model to infer generated sample quality.
We show that the proposed score correlates highly with the sample quality for various generative models including VAEs, GANs and Latent Diffusion Models.
In this paper, we propose to assess sample quality from another perspective: instead of using a pre-trained feature space, we directly use the latent space of the generative models themselves.

paper.title: Evaluating Generative Models for Tabular Data: Novel Metrics and Benchmarking
paper.abstract: Generative models have revolutionized multiple domains, yet their application to tabular data remains underexplored. Evaluating generative models for tabular data presents unique challenges due to structural complexity, large-scale variability, and mixed data types, making it difficult to intuitively capture intricate patterns. Existing evaluation metrics offer only partial insights, lacking a comprehensive measure of generative performance. To address this limitation, we propose three novel evaluation metrics: FAED, FPCAD, and RFIS. Our extensive experimental analysis, conducted on three standard network intrusion detection datasets, compares these metrics with established evaluation methods such as Fidelity, Utility, TSTR, and TRTS. Our results demonstrate that FAED effectively captures generative modeling issues overlooked by existing metrics. While FPCAD exhibits promising performance, further refinements are necessary to enhance its reliability. Our proposed framework provides a robust and practical approach for assessing generative models in tabular data applications.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper directly tackles the likelihood-free evaluation problem by proposing sample-based evaluation metrics (FAED, FPCAD, RFIS) for generative models whose learned distribution is not explicitly accessible, i.e., models that can sample but not compute likelihoods. It adapts FID-like and IS-like principles to tabular data and benchmarks the new metrics against SDV Fidelity, Utility, TSTR, and TRTS on three intrusion-detection datasets under injected quality decrease, mode drop, and mode collapse, finding FAED the most robust. This is a concrete instance of the requested evaluation methodology, but scoped to tabular generative models.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap is general ("likelihood-free generative models" across domains), whereas this paper provides evaluation metrics only for tabular data, and only validates them on network intrusion detection datasets; the authors themselves call for extending FAED/RFIS beyond this domain. Moreover, the validation protocol does not evaluate outputs of actual trained likelihood-free generative models — instead it injects noise/mode drop/mode collapse into real test data and checks metric sensitivity — so evidence on real generative-model outputs remains open. Finally, the proposed metrics are not fully reliable solutions: FPCAD is inconsistent across datasets and RFIS is unreliable for mode drop, so a robust, generally applicable likelihood-free evaluation method is still not established.
evidence_snippets: Since the model's learned distribution is not explicitly accessible, direct validation becomes impractical.
Inspired by IS and FID, we introduce three novel evaluation metrics, FAED, FPCAD, and RFIS, tailored for assessing generative models in tabular data.
Among the proposed novel metrics, FAED emerged as the most robust, consistently detecting structural distortions in generated data across various degradation scenarios.

paper.title: Evaluation Metrics and Methods for Generative Models in the Wireless PHY Layer
paper.abstract: Generative models are typically evaluated by direct inspection of their generated samples, e.g., by visual inspection in the case of images. Further evaluation metrics like the Fréchet inception distance or maximum mean discrepancy are intricate to interpret and lack physical motivation. These observations make evaluating generative models in the wireless PHY layer non-trivial. This work establishes a framework consisting of evaluation metrics and methods for generative models applied to the wireless PHY layer. The proposed metrics and methods are motivated by wireless applications, facilitating interpretation and understandability for the wireless community. In particular, we propose a spectral efficiency analysis for validating the generated channel norms and a codebook fingerprinting method to validate the generated channel directions. Moreover, we propose an application cross-check to evaluate the generative model's samples for training machine learning-based models in relevant downstream tasks. Our analysis is based on real-world measurement data and includes the Gaussian mixture model, variational autoencoder, diffusion model, and generative adversarial network as generative models. Our results under a fair comparison in terms of model architecture indicate that solely relying on metrics like the maximum mean discrepancy produces insufficient evaluation outcomes. In contrast, the proposed metrics and methods exhibit consistent and explainable behavior.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes three sample-only evaluation routines for generative models trained on wireless PHY channel data: (1) a spectral-efficiency analysis (empirical SE CDFs + Wasserstein distance) that validates generated channel norms, (2) a codebook-fingerprinting method (histograms over DFT-codebook indices compared via total variation distance) that validates generated channel directions, and (3) an application cross-check in which downstream models (GMM/VAE channel estimators and an autoencoder for channel compression) are trained on generated versus real (RPE) data and compared on the same test set. Because every routine uses only generated samples and never requires likelihood values, the framework is applicable to likelihood-free/implicit models and is demonstrated on GMM, VAE, diffusion model, and WGAN using real-world measurements.
assessments.what_remains_open: The research gap is generic: evaluation methods for likelihood-free generative models that sample without estimating likelihood. This paper provides a domain-specific instantiation only — all proposed metrics and methods are tied to wireless PHY channel data and its physical structure (channel-norm-driven SE, DFT-codebook direction histograms, communications downstream tasks such as channel estimation/compression). It does not provide a general, domain-agnostic evaluation methodology or transferable principle for assessing arbitrary likelihood-free generative models (e.g., image/text/tabular data), nor statistical guarantees or sample-complexity bounds for the proposed checks. Within wireless PHY it also evaluates one measurement scenario/config, and the authors note the rankings depend on the system configuration, so a generally applicable evaluation recipe for likelihood-free models remains open.
evidence_snippets: As a result, there is no clear guideline for assessing the quality of a generated channel with an established metric. Therefore, we propose a framework consisting of several evaluation metrics and methods for generative models in this work that are specifically suited for wireless channel data.

We propose an \ac{se} analysis and codebook fingerprinting as evaluation routines, allowing us to assess whether the generative model can capture two important channel properties for PHY layer algorithms: the overall channel power and directional information.

We introduce a general framework for an application cross-check. The cross-check enables us to determine if a generative model can be utilized in place of the true \ac{rpe} data for training \ac{ml}-based PHY layer methods and generate authentic channels.
